title: Functions, the math library, and errors
goal: Write functions that compute with loops, use <math.h> and <stdlib.h> (linking with -lm last), report errors on standard error with exit status 1, and sum a series: everything Assignment 4's sin.c needs.

topics.title: Functions in more depth
topics.examNote: Exam questions often say *write a function that...*: get the header (return type, name, parameter types) exactly right, and remember that a function must be **declared before it is used**.

blocks.text:
On Day 2 you wrote small functions. Today you will write functions that *compute* something with a loop, because that is what Assignment 4's `sin.c` needs.

### Declaration (prototype) and definition

C reads your file from top to bottom. A function must be **declared** before the line that calls it, so the compiler can check the call: the right number of arguments, and what type comes back.

- A **prototype** (also called a *function declaration*) is the header followed by a semicolon: `double cube(double x);`. It says the function exists, what it returns, and what it takes.
- A **definition** is the header followed by a body in `{ }`. It is the actual code.

You can either define the function above `main`, or put a prototype above `main` and the definition below it. Both are fine; the prototype style lets `main` come first so it is easy to find.

blocks.caption: proto.c: prototype above main, definition below

blocks.text: Notice `cube(2.0) + cube(-1.0)`: a function call that returns a value can be used anywhere a value of that type can go, such as inside a bigger expression or directly as a `printf` argument. Here it is 8.0 + (-1.0) = 7.0.

If you delete the prototype and keep the definition *below* `main`, gcc does not know `cube` yet. It prints `warning: implicit declaration of function 'cube'` and then `error: conflicting types for 'cube'`, because it guessed that the unknown function returns `int`. Fix: add the prototype, or move the definition above `main`.

### Parameters are copies

When you call `add_one(n)`, C copies the *value* of `n` into the parameter. The parameter is a **local variable** of the function: it exists only while the function runs, and changing it never changes the caller's variable. (Variables declared inside a function are local too; they are created on each call and must be given a starting value.)

blocks.caption: copies.c

blocks.code:
$ ./copies
inside add_one: n = 6
in main: n = 5

blocks.q: In copies.c, why does main still print 5?
blocks.a: `add_one` received a copy of the value 5 in its own parameter `n`. It changed the copy to 6. `main`'s `n` is a different variable and was never touched. To get a result *back* from a function, `return` it.

blocks.text:
### Return types and a loop inside a function

The return type is written before the name. Use `unsigned int` for a count that is never negative, and `double` for anything with a fractional part. A very common pattern is the **running total**: start a local variable at 0 (or at 1 for a product), update it in a loop, and return it at the end.

blocks.caption: loops.c: two functions that compute a result with a loop

blocks.text: `double total;` without `= 0.0` leaves `total` holding whatever garbage was in memory (the notebook's `sum_of.c` bug). Always initialize a running total. For a product, start at 1, not 0.
Inside `harmonic`, `1 / k` would be **integer division** (Day 2): 1/2 is 0. Writing `1.0 / k` makes it double division.

### Key points

- Prototype = header + `;`. Definition = header + body. Declare before you call.
- Parameters and local variables are copies that live only during the call; use `return` to send a result back.
- Return type comes first: `double f(...)`, `unsigned int g(...)`, `void h(...)` (returns nothing).
- Running total: initialize (0 for sums, 1 for products), update in a loop, return.
- A call that returns a value can be used inside any expression: `f(2) + f(3)`.

topics.title: <math.h>, <stdlib.h>, and error messages
topics.examNote: Know the usage-message pattern by heart: check `argc`, `fprintf(stderr, ...)`, exit status 1. Also know that `atof` gives 0.0 for text that is not a number.

blocks.text:
### `<math.h>`: pow, sqrt, fabs

The math library has functions much like Java's `Math` class. All of these take and return `double`:

| Function | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `sqrt(x)` | square root | `sqrt(2.0)` is 1.414214 |
| `pow(x, y)` | x to the power y | `pow(2.0, 10)` is 1024.0 |
| `fabs(x)` | absolute value of a double | `fabs(-3.5)` is 3.5 |

C has no overloading, so `fabs` is for doubles; there is a separate `abs` (in `<stdlib.h>`) for `int`.

blocks.caption: mathdemo.c

blocks.text:
### Linking with `-lm`, and why it goes LAST

`#include <math.h>` only gives the compiler the *prototypes*. The actual code of `pow` and `sqrt` is in a separate library file, the **math library**. You ask gcc to **link** it (join it into your program) with `-lm` (hyphen, lower-case L, m).

The **order matters** on Ubuntu (the CASLab machines and your VM). The linker reads the command line left to right. When it reaches `-lm` it only takes the functions that the files it has *already* seen are missing. If `-lm` comes before your `.c` file, nothing is missing yet, so it takes nothing; then your file asks for `sqrt` and `pow` and it is too late:

blocks.code:
$ gcc -Wall -o mathdemo -lm mathdemo.c
/usr/bin/ld: /tmp/ccshDxlJ.o: in function `main':
mathdemo.c:(.text+0x30): undefined reference to `sqrt'
/usr/bin/ld: mathdemo.c:(.text+0x68): undefined reference to `pow'
/usr/bin/ld: mathdemo.c:(.text+0xa0): undefined reference to `pow'
collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status

blocks.text: The Assignment 4 handout writes `gcc -o sin -lm sin.c`. On Ubuntu that gives exactly this ``undefined reference to `pow'`` error. Use **`gcc -Wall -o sin sin.c -lm`**: libraries after the source file. Forgetting `-lm` completely gives the same error.

### `<stdlib.h>`: atof and atoi

Command line arguments are always **strings** (Day 3): `argv[1]` for `./prog 2.5` is the text `"2.5"`, not a number. To do arithmetic you convert it:

- `atof(s)` (*ASCII to float*) converts a string to a `double`.
- `atoi(s)` (*ASCII to int*) converts a string to an `int`.

They read as much of the start of the string as looks like a number and ignore the rest. If the string does not start with a number they return **0** (0.0 for `atof`). They never print an error.

blocks.caption: conv.c

blocks.q: What does `atof("abc")` return, and what does that mean for a program run as `./prog abc`?
blocks.a: It returns 0.0. The program does not crash or complain; it simply computes with x = 0.0. (The Assignment 4 examples rely on this: `./sin abc` behaves like `./sin 0`.)

blocks.text:
### Errors: standard error and exit status

Every program has two output streams. **Standard output** (`stdout`) is for the program's normal results; `printf` and `puts` write there. **Standard error** (`stderr`) is for error messages. `fprintf` is `printf` with one extra first argument, the stream: `fprintf(stderr, "Usage: circle radius\n");`.

This is the Bash idea you already know: `>` redirects stdout, `2>` redirects stderr, and `$?` is the exit status of the last command. Sending errors to stderr means `./prog > results.txt` still shows the error on the screen, and does not mix it into the results.

The usual pattern: if `argc` is wrong, print a **usage message** (how to run the program) to stderr and exit with status 1 (any non-zero status means *failure*; 0 means success).

blocks.caption: circle.c: area of a circle from a radius on the command line

blocks.code:
$ gcc -Wall -o circle circle.c
$ ./circle 2
12.5664
$ echo $?
0
$ ./circle
Usage: circle radius
$ echo $?
1
$ ./circle 1 2 2> err.txt
$ echo $?
1
$ cat err.txt
Usage: circle radius

blocks.text:
`argc` counts the program name too, so *one* argument means `argc == 2`. In the `2> err.txt` run the message went into the file instead of the screen, which proves it was written to stderr.

### `exit(1)` versus `return 1`

`return 1;` ends the *current function*. Only in `main` does that also end the program with status 1. `exit(1);` (from `<stdlib.h>`) ends the **whole program** immediately with status 1, from *any* function. The course notebooks also write `exit(EXIT_FAILURE)`; `EXIT_FAILURE` is a name for a failure status (1 on Linux).

blocks.caption: exitdemo.c: exit from a helper function

blocks.code:
$ gcc -Wall -o exitdemo exitdemo.c
$ ./exitdemo hi
you typed hi
$ ./exitdemo
Usage: exitdemo word
$ echo $?
1

blocks.text: Writing the usage message with `printf` puts it on standard output. It looks the same on screen, but a checker (and the TAs) can tell: the message is in the wrong stream. Use `fprintf(stderr, ...)`.
Printing the message but forgetting `return 1` / `exit(1)`: the program keeps going and uses `argv[1]`, which may not exist. Reading past the end of `argv` is undefined behaviour.

### Key points

- `#include <math.h>` for `pow`, `sqrt`, `fabs`; compile with `-lm` **after** the `.c` file.
- `#include <stdlib.h>` for `atof`, `atoi`, `exit`. `atof("abc")` is 0.0, no error.
- Errors go to stderr: `fprintf(stderr, "Usage: prog x\n");`. Bash: `2>` redirects it, `$?` shows the status.
- Wrong number of arguments: check `argc != 2` (for one argument), print usage, exit status 1.
- `return 1` leaves the current function; `exit(1)` ends the program from anywhere.

topics.title: Summing a series (and a plan for sin.c)
topics.examNote: Assignment 4 is graded: this lesson teaches the skills with e^x and ln 2 examples and gives a plan in words. Write `sin.c` yourself.

blocks.text:
A **series** is a sum of many terms that follow a pattern. Computers compute many math functions by adding up the first few terms of a series. In code that is just a running total in a loop.

### Alternating signs

Some series alternate: +, -, +, -, ... For example 1 - 1/2 + 1/3 - 1/4 + ... gets closer and closer to ln 2. The simplest way to get the signs is a `sign` variable that starts at +1.0 and is flipped with `sign = -sign` after each term.

blocks.caption: ln2.c: an alternating series compared with the library's log

blocks.text: `%24.17f` (Day 2) prints 17 digits after the point in a field 24 characters wide, so you can see tiny differences. More terms get closer to ln 2 = 0.69314718..., but a finite number of terms is never exactly equal to it.

### Worked example: e to the power x

The exponential function has the series

e^x = 1 + x + x^2/2! + x^3/3! + x^4/4! + ...

where n! (*n factorial*) is 1 × 2 × ... × n, and 0! = 1. Every term has the form x^n / n!.

You could compute each term from scratch with `pow` and a factorial. This example uses a different trick: **each term is the previous term times x / n**. For example, x^3/3! = (x^2/2!) × x / 3. So the loop keeps one running `term` and one running `total`.

blocks.caption: exp.c: approximating e^x with the first terms of its series

blocks.q: Suppose you computed n! on its own in a loop, as an `int`. Why would that go wrong for the larger terms?
blocks.a: Factorials grow very fast. 12! = 479001600 still fits in an `int`, but 13! = 6227020800 is larger than the biggest `int` (2147483647). Signed `int` overflow is undefined behaviour, so the result could be anything. Doing the product in a `double` avoids this: a `double` holds 13!, 20! and much larger values (approximately, but very accurately at these sizes).

blocks.q: Why is the 21-term answer still not exactly equal to the library's `exp(1.0)`?
blocks.a: Two reasons. **Truncation**: we stopped after a finite number of terms, so we left out a (tiny) remainder. **Rounding**: a `double` holds about 16 significant decimal digits, so every division and addition is rounded a little, and those roundings add up. The library uses a cleverer method, so the last digit or two differ. That is expected.

blocks.text:
### Plan for Assignment 4's sin.c (in words; you write the code)

`sin.c` approximates sin(x) with the series x - x^3/3! + x^5/5! - x^7/7! + ... using the terms from x^1/1! up to x^13/13!. Every skill is in today's lessons. Steps:

1. Include the headers you need: `<stdio.h>` for printing, `<stdlib.h>` for `atof`, `<math.h>` for `pow`.
2. In `main(int argc, char *argv[])`, check the argument count first. Exactly one argument means `argc` must be 2. Otherwise print a usage message to **stderr** and end with exit status 1.
3. Convert `argv[1]` to a `double` with `atof`. (Non-numbers become 0.0; that is fine.)
4. Write the factorial function the assignment asks for (`fact`): multiply 1 × 2 × ... × n in a loop, keeping the product in a `double` and returning it (see the *Why?* box above for the reason). Note that `exp.c` used a running term instead, so the assignment's `fact` is yours to write.
5. Add up the terms in a loop with a running total. Think about two things: which powers appear (only the **odd** ones, 1, 3, 5, ..., 13; seven terms), and the **sign** of each term (+ for x^1, - for x^3, + for x^5, ...). Each term is the sign times `pow(x, n)` divided by `fact(n)`.
6. Print the result with exactly the format the assignment gives, `%24.17f` followed by a newline.
7. Compile with `-lm` **last**: `gcc -Wall -o sin sin.c -lm`.

Self-check by hand: the series at x = 0 is 0, and for small x the answer is very close to x (the assignment's example `./sin -0.01` prints `-0.00999983333416666`).

Common sin.c mistakes: (1) factorial in `int`, which overflows at 13!; (2) the wrong sign pattern, e.g. starting with minus, or flipping the sign at the wrong place; (3) one term too many or too few (stop at the x^13 term); (4) `%f` or `%.17f` instead of `%24.17f`, so the spacing does not match; (5) usage message on stdout or exit status 0; (6) `-lm` before `sin.c`.

Your answer will differ slightly from the library's `sin(x)` in the last digits, for the truncation and rounding reasons above. That is correct. The checker compares with what the *series* gives, not with `sin()`, so do not call `sin` from `<math.h>`.

Make the folder and write the program: `mkdir -p ~/CISC220_A4 && cd ~/CISC220_A4 && nano sin.c`. Compile with `gcc -Wall -o sin sin.c -lm` and try `./sin 0.5`, `./sin`, `./sin 1 2; echo $?`. Then run the checker: `cd ~/CISC220_current/c-app/drills && ./cdrill.sh a4 ~/CISC220_A4 sin.c`.

### Key points

- Series in code = running total in a loop; each pass adds one term.
- Alternating signs: `sign` starts at 1.0, then `sign = -sign` after each term.
- Factorials and powers get huge: use `double`, not `int`.
- A truncated series plus rounding differs from the library function in the last digits; that is expected.
- Print with `%24.17f` to see (and match) 17 decimal places.

flashcards.front: What is a function prototype? Give one.
flashcards.back: The function's header followed by a semicolon, with no body. It declares the return type, name and parameter types so the function can be called before its definition. Example: `double cube(double x);`
Prototype (declaration): header + `;`. Definition: header + `{ body }`. A function must be declared (by either) before the line that calls it.

flashcards.front: What happens to the caller's variable if a function changes its parameter?
flashcards.back: Nothing. Parameters are copies of the argument values (local variables of the function).

flashcards.front: How do you get a result out of a function?
flashcards.back: `return` it, and give the function a matching return type, e.g. `double f(...)` then `return total;`.

flashcards.front: Running-total pattern for a sum and for a product?
flashcards.back: Sum: `double total = 0.0;` then `total = total + term;` in the loop. Product: start at `1.0` and multiply. Return at the end.

flashcards.front: gcc says `implicit declaration of function 'f'`. Why?
flashcards.back: `f` is called before it is declared. Add a prototype above the call or move the definition above it.

flashcards.front: Which header and link flag for `pow`, `sqrt`, `fabs`?
flashcards.back: `#include <math.h>` and `-lm` at the END: `gcc -Wall -o prog prog.c -lm`.

flashcards.front: Why does `gcc -o sin -lm sin.c` fail on Ubuntu?
flashcards.back: The linker reads left to right; at `-lm` nothing needs `pow` yet, so it takes nothing. Then sin.c needs `pow`: ``undefined reference to `pow'``. Put `-lm` after the source file.
0.0, 2.5 and 7. They convert the number at the start of the string and ignore the rest; no number gives 0.

flashcards.front: How do you print an error message in C?
flashcards.back: `fprintf(stderr, "Usage: prog x\n");` writes to standard error instead of standard output.

flashcards.front: Usage check for a program that needs exactly one argument?
flashcards.back: `if (argc != 2) { fprintf(stderr, "Usage: prog x\n"); return 1; }` (argc counts the program name).
`return 1` ends the current function (the program only if it is `main`). `exit(1)` (stdlib.h) ends the whole program from any function, status 1.

flashcards.front: Bash: hide a program's error messages; see its exit status.
flashcards.back: `./prog 2> /dev/null` redirects stderr. `echo $?` prints the last exit status.

flashcards.front: How do you make the signs alternate +, -, +, ... in a loop?
flashcards.back: `double sign = 1.0;` and after adding each term, `sign = -sign;`.

flashcards.front: Why must a factorial function return `double`?
flashcards.back: 13! = 6227020800 is bigger than the largest `int` (2147483647); signed overflow is undefined behaviour. A `double` holds it.

flashcards.front: Two reasons a series answer differs from the library function.
flashcards.back: Truncation (only finitely many terms) and rounding (a double has about 16 significant digits; every operation rounds).
A double with 17 digits after the decimal point, right-aligned in a field at least 24 characters wide.

quiz.explain: `twice` doubles its own copy of `x` and returns 3.0. `main`'s `x` is unchanged, so it is still 1.5.
`odd_product(7)` multiplies 1 × 3 × 5 × 7 = 105. `odd_product(1)` is 1 and `odd_product(4)` is 1 × 3 = 3, so the sum is 4.
`n / 2` with `int n = 7` is integer division: 3. Only then is 3 converted to the return type `double`, giving 3.0. Write `n / 2.0` to get 3.5.

quiz.q: Which line is a function prototype?
quiz.explain: A prototype is the header followed by a semicolon. Option B is a definition; C and D are calls.

quiz.q: A function `void reset(int x) { x = 0; }` is called as `reset(count);`. Explain why `count` does not become 0.
quiz.answer: C passes arguments by value: `x` is a new local variable holding a copy of `count`'s value. Setting `x` to 0 changes only the copy, which disappears when `reset` returns.
quiz.explain: To change something for the caller, return a new value (`count = reset_value();`) or (later in the course) use a pointer.
`atof` reads the leading `2.5` and ignores `kg`; `atoi` reads the leading `2` and stops at the `.`. `"kg2.5"` does not start with a number, so `atof` returns 0.0.

quiz.q: This program is compiled as `prog` and run as `./prog 2> /dev/null`. What appears on the terminal?
quiz.explain: `puts` writes to standard output, which still goes to the terminal. `fprintf(stderr, ...)` writes to standard error, which `2> /dev/null` throws away.

quiz.q: On Ubuntu, which command builds `sin` from `sin.c`, which calls `pow`?
quiz.explain: The math library must come after the source file, because the linker reads left to right and only takes from a library what earlier files are missing. The other three fail with ``undefined reference to `pow'``.

quiz.q: Write the lines at the start of `main` for a program `temp` that needs exactly one command line argument: on a wrong count it prints `Usage: temp celsius` to standard error and ends with exit status 1.
quiz.explain: `argc` includes the program name, so one argument means `argc == 2`. `exit(1);` instead of `return 1;` is also correct (include `<stdlib.h>`).

quiz.q: What is the difference between `exit(1)` and `return 1`?
quiz.answer: `return 1` ends only the function it is in (it ends the program only when that function is `main`). `exit(1)` ends the whole program immediately with exit status 1, from any function.
quiz.explain: That is why a helper like `usage()` calls `exit(1)`: a `return` there would just go back to `main`.
The terms are +1 - 2 + 3 - 4 + 5 = 3. `sign` starts at 1 and flips after each term.
`%8.3f` gives 3 decimals right-aligned in 8 characters: three spaces then `1.414`. `%.0f` rounds to no decimals: 1.

quiz.q: A student's factorial helper returns `int`. Their series program is fine for small terms but goes wrong at 13!. Why, and what is the fix?
quiz.answer: 13! = 6227020800 does not fit in an `int` (largest 2147483647). Signed integer overflow is undefined behaviour, so the value is garbage. Fix: do the product in a `double` and return `double`.
quiz.explain: `unsigned int` does not help either: its largest value is 4294967295, still less than 13!.

write.prompt: Write a complete program `cube.c`. It takes exactly one command line argument x and prints x cubed with three decimal places, e.g. `./cube 1.5` prints `3.375`. Use a function `double cube(double x)` that is declared with a prototype above `main` and defined below it. If the number of arguments is wrong, print `Usage: cube x` to standard error and end with exit status 1.
write.explain: The prototype `double cube(double x);` lets `main` call `cube` before its definition. `main` checks `argc != 2` first (the program name counts), prints the usage message with `fprintf(stderr, ...)` and returns 1. Then `atof` converts the string `argv[1]` to a double (it needs `<stdlib.h>`), and the result of `cube(x)` is used directly as a `printf` argument with `%.3f`. No `-lm` is needed because nothing from `<math.h>` is used.

rubric.item: prototype above main and matching definition `double cube(double x)` returning x * x * x
usage message with `fprintf(stderr, ...)` and exit status 1

pitfalls: Checking `argc != 1`: argc counts the program name.
Using `printf` for the usage message (wrong stream).
Using `argv[1]` directly in arithmetic: it is a string.

write.prompt: Complete the function `alt_squares`, which returns the sum of the first n terms of 1 - 1/4 + 1/9 - 1/16 + ... (term k is 1/(k*k), with signs +, -, +, ...). With the main below the program prints 1.000000, 0.750000, 0.861111.

rubric.item: running total starts at 0.0 and is returned
adds sign / (k * k) using double division
flips the sign after each term

pitfalls: `1 / (k * k)` is integer division: 0 for every k > 1.
Flipping the sign before adding the first term makes the series start with minus.

write.prompt: Write a complete program `biggest.c` that prints the largest of its command line arguments, each converted with `atof`, using `printf("%f\n", ...)`. Any number of arguments (one or more) is allowed: `./biggest 3 -7.5 12.25 4` prints `12.250000`. With no arguments, print a usage message to standard error and end with exit status 1.

no arguments (`argc < 2`): usage message on stderr and exit status 1
starts the maximum at the first argument (not at 0, which fails for all-negative input)
